query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The formation and crystal-structure selection of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles in a single-phase solid-solution state are governed by the combined effects of rapid heating and cooling rates, and the high entropy of mixing, which stabilizes the solid solution and prevents phase separation.
generation.intervention: rapid heating and cooling synthesis regimes
generation.conditions: heating temperature of ~2000 K, cooling rate of ~104 K/s
generation.mechanism: stabilization of solid solution and prevention of phase separation
generation.predicted_outcome: formation of single-phase nanoparticles with uniform elemental mixing
generation.boundary: heating and cooling rates, composition of the alloy
generation.uncertainty: effects of specific noble metals and their combinations on the formation and crystal-structure selection

falsification_experiment.design: synthesis of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles using rapid heating and cooling rates, with varying compositions and heating/cooling conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the resulting nanoparticles exhibit significant phase separation or non-uniform elemental mixing, the hypothesis is falsified, with a threshold of >10% phase separation or >5% variation in elemental composition

cited_evidence.text: These methods require high reaction temperatures, and rapid cooling to maintain a high-entropy state at room temperature. As a result, the preparation of high-entropy nanoparticles with a single solid solution can be achieved in a non-equilibrium state by suppressing the formation of secondary phases. In 2018, a carbothermal shock method was reported by Yao et al. to alloy up to eight elements into HEA NPs with the designated composition and size. This method involves a 55-ms heating of mixed metal precursors on carbon supports at a peak temperature of 2000 K in argon and cooling at a cooling rate of ∼105 K/s. The high temperature ensures uniform mixtures of multiple elements by fission/fusion and catalytically driven particle dispersion mechanisms. This work has made an important step in the rapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles. However, this method can only be applied to conductive, surface-oxidized carbon support materials. Since then, more work has been reported on the rapid synthesis of HEA NPs within milliseconds to seconds, including fast-moving bed heating, electrical sparkling, Joule heating and microwave heating. To synthesize the MPEI nanoparticles, we preloaded a carbon substrate with desired metal salt precursor combinations/ratios and Joule-heated (fig. S5) the materials with precise control of the temperature and heating/cooling rates by tuning the power applied to the substrate (fig. S6). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).
